manipuri_koubru.name: Guard the north-western quarter of the Kangleipak world
manipuri_koubru.notes: As one of the four cardinal Umang Lai, Koubru (Koupalu) is the omniscient guardian of the north-west, enthroned on the summit of Mount Koubru.

sources.reference: Mount Koubru / Koupalu, Wikipedia (citing Sanamahist tradition)

manipuri_kounu.name: Personify and protect Mount Kounu and the northern hills
manipuri_kounu.notes: Goddess who is the female personification of Mount Kounu and, with Koubru, watches over the northern Kanglei world.

sources.reference: Mount Koubru, Wikipedia (Kounu as personification of Mount Kounu)

manipuri_leimarel.name: Bring forth all living beings from her womb
manipuri_leimarel.notes: As the eternal earth-mother, men and women were believed to originate from the womb of Leimarel Sidabi.

manipuri_leimarel.name: Emanate the household goddess Emoinu from herself
manipuri_leimarel.notes: At the bidding of the creator Atingkok Maru Sidaba she produced from herself the goddess Emoinu, sent to earth as guardian of humankind and of the hearth.

manipuri_marjing.name: Invent the game of polo (sagol kangjei)
manipuri_marjing.notes: Parratt: Marjing's chief importance in Meitei mythology is that he is credited with the invention of polo, the national game; the first divine match was played at Lai Haraoba.

sources.reference: Marjing, Wikipedia (citing Saroj N. Arambam Parratt, The Religion of Manipur)

manipuri_marjing.name: Enter and reside within the human body as one of its souls
manipuri_marjing.notes: Marjing is reckoned one of the gods who enter the human body and position themselves there as a soul.

manipuri_nongpok_ningthou.name: Reign as sovereign guardian of the eastern direction
manipuri_nongpok_ningthou.notes: The 'King of the East', ruling guardian deity of the eastern quarter, enthroned on the Nongmaiching (Langmai) hills.

manipuri_panthoibi.name: Grant courage and victory in war
manipuri_panthoibi.notes: Warrior-goddess patroness of courage, victory and warfare, invoked for triumph in battle.

manipuri_panthoibi.name: Bestow civilization, handicraft and wisdom
manipuri_panthoibi.notes: Patroness of civilization, the handicrafts (especially weaving), fertility and wisdom in the Panthoibi Khonggul tradition.

manipuri_sanamahi.name: Guard the household and all mankind
manipuri_sanamahi.notes: Lainingthou Sanamahi is the supreme guardian god of the home and of humankind, worshipped daily in the south-western corner of every Meitei house.

sources.reference: Lainingthou Sanamahi, Simple English Wikipedia; Sanamahism, Wikipedia

manipuri_thangjing.name: Guard the south-western quarter and the Moirang realm
manipuri_thangjing.notes: Ancient ruling deity of Moirang and cardinal Umang Lai of the south-west, reigning on the banks of Loktak lake and protecting the southern Imphal valley.

manipuri_wangbren.name: Rule the rivers and the under-water world
manipuri_wangbren.notes: God of water, rain and flood, lord of the rivers and ruler of the under-water realm.

manipuri_wangbren.name: Send and withhold disease and sickness
manipuri_wangbren.notes: As lord of water and flood he is also the god of disease and sickness, propitiated to avert epidemics.

mangaian_tango.name: Hold lordship over the birds and over Enua-kura
mangaian_tango.notes: Third child of Vari-ma-te-takere, set to dwell at Enua-kura, the land of red parrot-feathers, as lord of birds (Gill 1876).

sources.reference: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific (1876), ch. I

mangaian_tumu_te_ana_oa.name: Be the living Echo dwelling in the caves of Mangaia
mangaian_tumu_te_ana_oa.notes: The personified Echo, fourth child of Vari, who dwells in and answers from the caves of Mangaia (Gill 1876).

sources.reference: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific (1876), ch. I

mangaian_tuna.name: Take the form of a handsome youth to woo Ina
mangaian_tuna.notes: Tuna, god of eels, transforms from eel to youth to become the lover of Ina near her cave at Tamarua (Gill 1876).

sources.reference: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific (1876), ch. V

mangaian_tuna.name: Yield the first coconut palm from his buried head
mangaian_tuna.notes: He bids Ina cut off his head and bury it; from it springs the first coconut palm, its three eye-marks held to be Tuna's face (Gill 1876).

sources.reference: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific (1876), ch. V

manipuri_pakhangba.name: The royal Pakhangba flag and coat of arms of Manipur

manipuri_marjing.name: Kangjei (polo stick) and kangdrum ball offered to him

sources.reference: Marjing, Wikipedia (offering of polostick/kangdrum at Heingang)

manipuri_salailen.name: The divine thunderbolt with which he smites evil spirits

sources.reference: Atingkok, Wikipedia (sky god who controls thunder and lightning)

manipuri_panthoibi.name: Sword and spear borne as a warrior-goddess

sources.reference: Panthoibi, Wikipedia; Panthoibi Khonggul (her warrior exploits)
Marjing, Wikipedia (god of polo and sport)
Names of the Supreme God in Meitei religion, Simple English Wikipedia; Atingkok, Wikipedia
Sidaba Mapu, Wikipedia; Names of the Supreme God in Meitei religion

manipuri_leimarel.gloss: the immortal great-lady of the earth

manipuri_thangjing.name: Moirang Lai Haraoba
manipuri_thangjing.notes: The great Lai Haraoba ('pleasing of the gods') for Thangjing at Moirang is among the longest of the tradition, its dances and rituals re-enacting the cosmogony and sometimes continuing for a month.

manipuri_marjing.name: Offering of the polo-stick at Heingang
manipuri_marjing.notes: Each year devotees ascend the Heingang (Marjing) hill to offer a polo-stick (kangdrum/kangjei) to the god, alongside his Lai Haraoba; the first divine polo match is said to have been played at Lai Haraoba.

manipuri_koubru.name: Koubru Ching Kaba (pilgrimage to Mount Koubru)
manipuri_koubru.notes: Meitei pilgrims ascend Mount Koubru to the summit shrine of Koupalu; the mountain is among the most visited pilgrimage sites of Sanamahism.

manipuri_sanamahi.name: Household worship at the Sanamahi Kachin
manipuri_sanamahi.notes: Every Meitei household maintains a Sanamahi corner (kachin) in the south-west, where Sanamahi and Leimarel are honoured daily with a lamp and incense on live charcoal, and fresh vegetables on festival days.

sources.reference: Lainingthou Sanamahi, Simple English Wikipedia; Sanamahism, Wikipedia

manipuri_leimarel.name: Hearth worship in the isaiphu and phunga lairu
manipuri_leimarel.notes: Leimarel (with Sanamahi) is worshipped in the first room of every Meitei home, present in an isaiphu (earthen water-pitcher) with no image; her hearth aspect is the phunga lairu, the sacred kitchen fire.

sources.reference: Leimarel Sidabi, Wikipedia; Imoinu / Emoinu, Grokipedia

manipuri_wangbren.name: Worship at the Sugnu shrine
manipuri_wangbren.notes: The chief cult-centre of Wangbren is the shrine at Sugnu; non-Christian Anal villagers annually give offerings to a priest who presents them to the god there.

manipuri_nongpok_ningthou.name: Lai Haraoba of the divine union
manipuri_nongpok_ningthou.notes: The union of Nongpok Ningthou and Panthoibi on the Nongmaiching hills, celebrated with dance and music by the gods, is held to be the origin of the Lai Haraoba festival itself.

manipuri_panthoibi.name: Lai Haraoba and the Panthoibi rites
manipuri_panthoibi.notes: Panthoibi is honoured in Lai Haraoba, whose origin is traced to her union with Nongpok Ningthou; her exploits are chanted from the Panthoibi Khonggul.

mari_keche.name: Grove-prayer to the sun among the heaven-gods
mari_keche.notes: Keče is propitiated together with the other heaven-gods at the communal grove (küsoto) festivals of Mari native religion, which involve prayer and animal sacrifice.

mansi_numi_torum.name: Reindeer sacrifice at sacred sites
mansi_numi_torum.notes: Numi-Torum is honoured with offerings of reindeer at sacred sites and communal feasts among the Mansi, the blood and organs presented at shrines.

sources.reference: Num-Torum, Wikipedia; Mansi religion ethnography (Munkácsi corpus)

mangaian_rongo.name: Human sacrifice and taro offering at Orongo and Akaoro marae
mangaian_rongo.notes: At Orongo marae a human victim was laid on a block of limestone before Rongo's image, especially to secure victory in war; in peacetime parcels of cooked taro were his regular offering at the inland Akaoro marae.

sources.reference: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific (1876)

attributes.name: Paphal (coiled ouroboros-like dragon-serpent)
attributes.notes: Post-Khagemba representations show Pakhangba as a paphal, a serpent/dragon coiled and biting or nearing its own tail, symbol of cosmic energy and balance in Lai Haraoba.

attributes.name: Serpent bearing the antlers of the sangai (brow-antlered deer)
attributes.notes: He is figured as a great serpent or python crowned with sangai antlers, fusing the serpent and stag totems.

attributes.name: Mounted on the winged steed Samadon Ayangba
attributes.notes: Marjing is depicted with his divine winged horse Samadon Ayangba (Hada Samaton Ayangba), companion on the Heingang hill.

sacredAnimals.name: Horse (the Manipuri pony) and the winged steed

attributes.name: Axe with which he fells the Wazacá tree of life
attributes.notes: The culture-hero's defining act is felling the primordial Wazacá tree, whose stump becomes Mount Roraima and whose felling looses the world-flood that recreates humanity.

sources.reference: Pemon, Wikipedia; Macuxi, Indigenous Peoples in Brazil (pib.socioambiental.org)

sacredAnimals.name: Reindeer (the sacrificial victim offered to him)

attributes.name: Luminous flying fireball / orb of light by night
attributes.notes: Appears as a small child or, transformed, as a bright flying orb of fire, often likened to a will-o'-the-wisp.

attributes.name: Manifest in volcano, thunder, lightning and earthquake
attributes.notes: The Pillañ, ancestral spirits of dead chiefs and warriors, inhabit volcanoes and show themselves in eruption, thunder, lightning and earthquake; the volcanoes are thereby sacred.

sources.reference: Mapuche religion, Wikipedia; Pillan, Garland Magazine

attributes.name: Giant eel whose buried head sprouts the coconut
attributes.notes: Tuna appears as the great eel; the three eye-and-mouth marks on every coconut shell are explained as his face, the white flesh as 'Tuna's brains'.

sources.reference: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific (1876), ch. V
